solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: China police ran amok

indicators.note: running amok is going wild and out of control, so these letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A riot in China, with the police running wild in the streets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country, but the capital is only there to start the clue; it means fine crockery. 'Ran' is fodder as well as part of the phrase 'ran amok'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lowercase china is fine ceramic tableware, and porcelain is the material it is made from, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Ring friend about opening of exhibition

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so only that one is kept
to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: a pal is a friend
first letter of exhibition

explanation.surface: Phoning a friend about the opening night of an exhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' reads as a phone call, but the answer is the sound of bells. PAL is split to hold the E.
explanation.definitionFit: A peal is a loud ringing of bells, so as a noun it is a synonym for a ring.

clue.text: Selfish driver travelled in unusual way, I hear

indicators.note: what is heard rather than read is about sound, so the spelling may differ

blocks.note: to have ridden on a pig would be an unusual way to travel

explanation.surface: Complaining about a selfish motorist who was driving strangely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rode' is the past of ride, so travelling astride a hog is the odd journey; spoken, it matches the term for a bad driver.
explanation.definitionFit: A road hog is an idiom for a motorist who drives inconsiderately, hogging the lane and ignoring other drivers.

clue.text: I leave after end of June

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept
coming after something means being placed behind it in the line

blocks.note: last letter of June
to go is to leave

explanation.surface: Someone announcing they will quit once June is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' looks like the subject of the sentence, but it is the definition. The wordplay reads in reverse order: GO comes after E.
explanation.definitionFit: Ego is Latin for the first-person pronoun, and in psychology it names the conscious self, so it fits the pronoun.

clue.text: Declare south-east to be hostile

blocks.note: to aver is to declare or assert
SE is the compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: A political declaration that the south-east of the country is an enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: AVER is a formal word for state firmly, common in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Being averse means having a strong dislike or opposition to something, close in sense to unfriendly opposition.

clue.text: Self-obsessed youth Russians caught after disturbance

indicators.note: a disturbance throws things into disorder, so the letters come out rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A vain young man arrested by Russians following some unrest.
explanation.walkthrough: The C for caught joins the eight letters before they are all mixed together.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Narcissus was a beautiful young man who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool.

clue.text: Briefly train for a fight in Bath?

indicators.note: putting something briefly means cutting it short, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: boxers practise with a partner before a real bout

explanation.surface: A boxer training for a bout in a bathroom, or in the city of Bath.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath is an English city famous for its Roman hot springs; the question mark flags that it is one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bath is a celebrated spa town, so it stands as an example of a resort with mineral springs.

clue.text: State prosecutor featured in paper

indicators.note: whatever is featured in something appears inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: the Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
a DA is a district attorney, the US public prosecutor

explanation.surface: A state prosecutor appearing in the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State prosecutor' reads as one phrase, but 'State' alone is the definition, meaning a country.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudan is a sovereign nation in north-east Africa, and a state can mean any independent country.

clue.text: Cut short a card game

blocks.note: taken as written
bridge is a card game played by two pairs

explanation.surface: Bringing a game of cards to an early end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' sounds like cutting the deck before a game, but 'Cut short' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To abridge a book or speech is to shorten it by condensing or removing parts, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Seafood a bishop has all by himself

blocks.note: taken as written
B is the chess notation for bishop
someone all by himself is alone

explanation.surface: A bishop eating his seafood dinner without company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has' reads as eating, but it only joins the definition to the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Abalone is an edible sea snail prized in Asian and Californian cooking, an example of shellfish.

clue.text: It detects movement back and forth

indicators.note: reading the same going back and going forth describes a word that is unchanged either way

blocks.note: the definition also supplies the letters, which are unchanged when read in either direction

explanation.surface: Describing a sensor that picks up things moving to and fro.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back and forth' looks like part of the movement being detected, but it tells you the word reads the same in both directions.
explanation.definitionFit: Radar systems bounce radio waves off objects to locate aircraft, ships and speeding cars, sensing their motion.

clue.text: Tough, like a rhino perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: hard to hurt with criticism
second meaning: literally having a heavy hide, as that animal does

explanation.walkthrough: One sense is figurative, about someone insensitive to insults; the other is literal, and 'perhaps' shows the rhino is only one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes both a person unbothered by criticism and an animal with a heavy protective hide.

clue.text: Very many noblemen welcoming the French

indicators.note: welcoming someone means taking them in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: counts are European noblemen
les is the French plural word for the

explanation.surface: A crowd of aristocrats greeting their French guests.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural S of the noblemen is split off to close round the French article.
explanation.definitionFit: Countless means too numerous to be counted, so it is an idiomatic way of saying a huge number.

clue.text: Boat in which soldiers might find shelter

definitions.text: in which soldiers might find shelter

blocks.note: first meaning: a canoe hollowed from a single tree trunk

blocks.clueFragment: in which soldiers might find shelter
blocks.note: second meaning: a roofed trench used by troops for cover

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one description of a boat that houses troops, but it is two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a primitive canoe carved from a log and a covered pit giving troops protection in war.

clue.text: Sleeping with Rod upset male social worker

indicators.note: in a down clue, to upset is to turn upside down, so the word reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the standard abbreviation for male
ants live in colonies, so an ant is a social insect and worker

explanation.surface: Someone sleeping with Rod has upset a man who works in social services.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Social worker' suggests a caseworker, but it is the insect: ants are social, and many are workers.
explanation.definitionFit: Dormant describes something inactive or asleep, like a volcano or a hibernating animal, so it matches the adjective.

clue.text: Priest, a televangelist, pockets dead man’s assets

indicators.note: what one pockets is held inside, so the letters are tucked within the words

blocks.note: the run of letters straddles all three words

explanation.surface: A greedy TV preacher helps himself to a deceased man's wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma and the space are ignored when reading the letters through.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is the property and money a person leaves on death, administered by executors under a will.

clue.text: Encourage a new partner to go round India

indicators.note: going round something means encircling it, so pieces close in from both sides

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
a mate is a partner
India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Urging a fresh partner to travel around India.
explanation.walkthrough: The I sits in the gap between N and MATE, so 'a new partner' as a whole goes round it.
explanation.definitionFit: To animate someone is to give them life and spirit, so it can mean to enliven or inspire them.

clue.text: Two Englishmen down under making a gun

blocks.note: pom is Australian slang for an English person
the slang word is used a second time, as there are two of them

explanation.surface: Two English emigrants in Australia building a firearm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down under' means Australia, which tells you to use the Australian slang word for an English person.
explanation.definitionFit: A pom-pom is a rapid-firing automatic cannon, named for its sound, used against aircraft in both world wars.

clue.text: Love affair flourishing in Paris hotel

indicators.note: a flourish is an extravagant waving movement, so the letters are flung into a new pattern

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A romance blossoming in a hotel in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flourishing' looks like it describes the affair thriving, but it signals the mix of the letters that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A relationship is a romantic or sexual involvement between two people, the same thing as an affair of the heart.

clue.text: Writer embraced by fat Scottish landowner

indicators.note: something embraced by another is held in its arms, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: lard is pig fat
the writer of the clue refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: An author hugged by a stout Scottish laird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat' looks like an adjective describing the landowner, but it is a noun meaning cooking fat.
explanation.definitionFit: Laird is the Scots form of lord, used for a man owning a large estate in Scotland.

clue.text: Announcement of top dog

indicators.note: an announcement is spoken out loud, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a peak is the top of a mountain

explanation.surface: Naming the champion at a dog show, the top dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top dog' reads as a single phrase for the boss, but it splits into the sound clue and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Peke is the short informal name for a Pekingese, a small long-haired toy breed from China.

clue.text: Girl giving her name to a band?

definitions.text: Girl giving her name to a band?

blocks.clueFragment: Girl giving her name to a band?
blocks.note: surface reading: a woman who lends her name to a pop group
setter's reading: the band is a hairband, named after the heroine of a Lewis Carroll story

explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' suggests a music group, but it is a stretchy band worn over the head; this one is named after the girl in Tenniel's illustrations of Carroll's Wonderland books.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Wonderland wears a hair ribbon in the drawings, and that style of headband took her first name.

clue.text: Penny having a couple of beers — of this type?

definitions.text: Penny having a couple of beers — of this type?

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for penny
ale is beer, and a couple means two

explanation.surface: Penny is out at the pub, drinking two pints of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the drinks Penny has are of the kind the answer names, so the final words point back at the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Pale ale is a light-coloured beer brewed with pale malt, so it is a plausible type for the drinks.

clue.text: At heart, clown is quite sad

indicators.note: the heart of something is its centre, so only the middle letters are kept

blocks.note: middle three letters of clown

explanation.surface: The old idea that the clown is secretly melancholy underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first and last letters of the five-letter word are dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling low means being somewhat down or depressed, a mild version of sadness rather than despair.

clue.text: Regularly trendy youth in the 1950s

indicators.note: doing something regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters of trendy

explanation.surface: A fashionable young person from the 1950s.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trendy' seems to describe the youth, but it only supplies letters. A Ted, or Teddy boy, was a British youth in Edwardian-style suits in the 1950s.
explanation.definitionFit: Teddy boys were a 1950s British youth subculture, known for long drape jackets and rock and roll.

clue.text: Homes were wrecked at an unspecified location

indicators.note: something wrecked is broken apart, so its letters are left in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A news report of houses destroyed in some undisclosed place.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads like the end of a news sentence, so it is easy to miss that it is the answer's meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in or at a place not named or known, matching an undisclosed or unknown location.
